Overview

  • Western Australia: A mouse plague is under way across multiple regions. The worst outbreak is occurring in the Northern (Geraldton) zone, followed by another east from Fitzgerald in the Sandplain (Esperance) zone. Mouse abundance in Eastern (Kwinana East) / and Central (Kwinana West) zones appears to be low, but growers here should remain vigilant.

  • South Australia: Mouse activity is moderate across Adelaide Plains and Yorke Peninsula. We have observed a decrease in activity from last season, likely due to lower food availability and proactive management during sowing. However, mouse activity could increase as more food is now available.

  • Elsewhere: mouse numbers likely remain low.

  • An emergency permit has been issued by the APVMA for the higher dose ZnP50 bait. Locations with permit access change on a fortnightly basis, based on APVMA-defined current mouse activity categories (differing from our mouse forecasts, which are based on different data types, metrics and time periods). Check the GRDC website for emergency permit information and current access.

Management recommendations

  • Mouse activity should be monitored through winter in zones with moderate-high activity: WA Sandplain, WA Northern and SA Midnorth-Lower Yorke Eyre, and prepare to take action.

  • Monitor mice activity in crops using chew cards or a walk-through, searching for active mouse burrows and crop damage.

  • If you detect mice, consider applying zinc phosphide bait before crops mature, as bait will become less attractive to mice once grain develops in the head.

  • ZnP25 is the only currently registered bait available everywhere; use in accordance with the label instructions and report any adverse effects via the APVMA website. An emergency permit is currently available for the higher dose ZnP50 bait, check access and requirements on the GRDC website.

  • Plan for a clean harvest (minimal grain loss) to reduce mouse food through the stubble.

About

Mouse forecasts are enabled through a Grains Research and Development Corporation and CSIRO investment into the 2025-29 Mouse Monitoring and Surveillance project via the Rodent Pest Management team. Forecasts will be updated seasonally or as new data comes available.

We are actively developing new statistical models to improve mouse forecasts, and working on their presentation. This work is run in coordination with the National Mouse Group, a grower-led network of farmers, industry representatives, state government, GRDC and CSIRO. The group meet three times a year to update local reports of the current mouse situation, review management recommendations and determine research priorities.

Monitoring data

Mouse population surveys are conducted 2 - 3 times a year at each of the ~170 long-term monitoring sites. Mice are surveyed through active burrow searches and chew cards. To calibrate this data against more robust population density measurements, we also conduct live-trapping at 3 sites (Adelaide Plains SA, Northern Mallee VIC and Central West NSW).

Mouse monitoring data is collected by CSIRO, NSW Local Land Services, NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, Central West Farming Services, Birchip Cropping Group, & Farmanco. We also thank NSW DPIRD who generously provide additional live-trapping survey data. Further live-trapping data is also occasionally supplied through the GRDC / CSIRO Mouse Ecology 2024-2029 project.

We also receive reports from farmers, agronomists and other community members directly. This is key information we consider given we cannot feasibly survey every paddock across the entire grain growing region.

Report mouse activity

Take 60 seconds to report mouse activity on your farm on MouseAlert.

We incorporate observations of mouse activity (and reports of mouse damage) from farmers with our own monitoring surveys to create these forecasts and improve understanding of mouse populations, to help keep producers informed. We are primarily using observations of mouse activity within paddocks (not houses or farm sheds). If you have seen mice in your paddocks, report your observations into MouseAlert. If you’ve looked and found no mice, or low mouse activity, this information is also important to report as high mouse activity observations.
